The building itself is the old Board School annexe, leased from the town council for a peppercorn
rent on a lease that runs to 2047. It has a strong room that was once the coal store, a workroom that
was once a classroom, and a reading room that still has the pegs for coats along one wall. Nobody
has ever suggested removing the pegs, and nobody should; they are the last of the original fittings,
and the caretaker, who has been here longer than the archive, is fond of them.

provenance.key: Working Notes for the Millbrook Community Archive

These notes describe how the Millbrook Community Archive is run from week to week. They are
written for the volunteers who staff the reading room and process new material, and they assume
nothing beyond care, patience and a willingness to write things down. The archive holds the papers
of a small town: parish minutes, shop ledgers, school registers, photographs, and the
correspondence of families who never expected anyone to read it. None of it is valuable in the
auction sense, and all of it is irreplaceable.

The archive exists because the county record office is forty miles away and accepts only what it
judges to be of regional significance. A great deal of what matters to Millbrook falls below that line.
The founding committee decided in 1987 that the town would keep its own record, in its own
building, catalogued by its own people, and that decision has held through three moves of premises
and two floods. The collection now runs to roughly nine hundred boxes and grows by thirty or forty
a year.

Material arrives in three ways: by donation, by deposit and by rescue. A donation transfers
ownership to the archive outright. A deposit leaves ownership with the depositor and lends us
custody under written terms. A rescue is anything carried in from a skip, a house clearance or a
closing business, and it is treated as a donation until somebody with a better claim appears, which
in thirty years has happened twice, both times amicably and both times over a cup of tea.

Every accession, however it arrives, is logged on the day it comes through the door. The log records
the date, the source, a one-line description and the name of the volunteer who received it. It does
not attempt to describe the contents in detail; that is the job of cataloguing, which happens later
and often much later. What the log must do is make certain that nothing can be in the building
without a record of how it got there, and of who to ask about it.

Nothing is thrown away on arrival. Duplicates, blank forms and obvious rubbish are set aside in a
marked box and reviewed at the quarterly committee meeting, where the decision to dispose is
minuted. Volunteers acting alone have in the past discarded items that turned out to be the only
surviving copy, and the quarterly rule exists because of those occasions rather than in spite of them.
Patience here costs a shelf; haste costs a record, and the shelf is the cheaper of the two.

Depositors are given a receipt and a copy of the deposit terms, and the terms are kept simple: the
archive may catalogue, conserve and make the material available for research, and the depositor
may withdraw it on three months' notice. Longer or more elaborate agreements have been tried
and have always ended in confusion about what was actually promised, usually after the people
who made the promise had left the committee and taken their memory of the conversation with
them.
